utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Perhaps I could deal with one matter very briefly. It is about remaining issue from the testimony of Slavisa Sabljic. It is about P7052, -53, and -54. On the 23rd of January of this year during the testimony of Slavisa Sabljic, the Prosecution tendered three audio clips with 65 ter numbers 01643d, same number, small e, and same number, small c. The Defence objected but was unable to articulate grounds for its objection. The Chamber exceptionally marked the audio clips for identification, respectively as P7052, P7053, and P7054, and granted the Defence limited time to develop its objections. This can be found at transcript pages 30565 through 30566. As of today's date, the Defence has not made any further submissions with regard to its objection and therefore the Chamber will now decide on admission. The Chamber notes that these audio clips are, according to the Prosecution, tape recorded conversations between the accused and his subordinates, and Witness Sabljic testified that he recognised the voice of the accused on these audio clips. This can be found at transcript pages 30559, 30562, through 30564 and 30566. And therefore the Chamber finds that P7052, P7053, and P7054 are relevant and of probative value and admits them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, our apologies for continuing dealing with the matter we were dealing with when you entered the courtroom. We'll continue in a minute, but I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jeremy will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, yesterday in your diary and in Mr. Rasula's diary we looked at a list of names of leading non-Serbs in Sanski Most who were to be arrested or captured. Now, a number of these men were indeed captured, and they were made to appeal to their fellow non-Serb citizens over the public radio in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd look to look at some of those broadcasts now, or the transcript of those broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3302 on our screens. And if we could please go to page 5 in the English and page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see that this is a transcript of broadcasts made over the radio in Sanski Most during late May 1992, and I would like to direct your attention to the female voice identified on the page in front of you which reads as follows: "We call upon the inhabitants of Pobrijezje to bring all their weapons and military equipment to the cross-roads at the check-point by 1800 hours. If not, at exactly 1810 hours we will begin to shell the village. If the order is not complied with, we will not bear moral or material responsibility for the consequences of the shelling." Now, sir, Pobrijezje is familiar to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a village close to Sanski Most. About 2 or 3 kilometres away from town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now I would like to direct your attention to the male voice identified below the excerpt I just read out. We see that it reads as follows: "The Serbian armed forces captured the greatest Muslim and Croatian extremists in the Sanski Most municipality. Faik Biscevic who attempted to flee from the town." And it goes on to say that this extremists will address the Croatian and Muslim peoples over the radio. And I'd like to just look at a part of Faik Biscevic's address. So we see at the -- at the bottom of the page in the English: "Announcement. That all Muslims and Croats unconditionally hand over all the weapons they possess ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "... legally and illegally and that they surrender to the Serbian army and government because this is a Serbian town. To avoid the soldiers having to use force and locate and seize weapons, it would be better to hand over the weapons voluntarily, otherwise Sana/Sanski Most/will continue to be destroyed until final capitulation." So, Faik Biscevic, you mentioned him in your statement, and you actually mentioned him yesterday in connection with Dr. Mehmed Alagic saying that you considered Mehmed Alagic an extremist because he was under the influence of Faik Biscevic. Now, Mr. Biscevic was a fellow dentist in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And he was forced by the Serbian authorities to make this address, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. But he didn't work as a dentist. He was a goldsmith in town before the war. He didn't work at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this announcement -- well, yesterday you told this Court that the entry in your diary relating to the handing in of weapons applied to Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike and that it was only weapons held illegally for which documentation did not exist that had to be handed in. Now, it's very clear that this announcement is aimed only at Muslim and Croats and that it applies to both legal and illegal weapons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that illegal weapons were being taken away. Now I see here that it was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So this is the first time that - to your knowledge - non-Serbs were asked to hand in legally held weapons. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first time I hear that the legal ones were being taken away as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So yesterday when you said that you considered extremists to be persons with weapons, then, if I understand what you're saying today, then what you meant was that an extremist was someone who held a weapon illegally without the required documentation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Illegal. Who had illegal weapons. And that kind of thing did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I would like to change topic briefly. You were involved in sanitation activities following disarming operations in Sanski Most in late May and June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received evidence that Muslims killed during these operations were buried in common graves without the usual burial rights and in the absence of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's P2407.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you knew that Muslims were buried in this way; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards I heard that they were buried in a common grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you also hear that they were buried in the absence of their family?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the reason why they were buried in the absence of their family were because all of their family were locked up in various locations in Sanski Most at the time of their burial; yes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I could not say. Where they were, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's try and get to the bottom of where they were. And to do that, I'd like to look at your diary again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 19777. And if we could go to page 23, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see that this is another Crisis Staff meeting. It's on the 28th of May, 1992. First entry is: "- Exchange through Jajce." That's in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's above Sanski Most, over there towards Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Next entry we see: "Pobrijezje wants to move out voluntarily from the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most." Now, this is the same village that was warned over the radio that their village would be shelled if all weapons were not brought to a check-point; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pobrijezje? That's that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it's the same village referred to in the radio broadcast we just looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same village. There is no other one but that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, if you decide to leave your village in response to someone threatening to shell it, then that decision to leave is not really one you've taken voluntarily, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for a legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It asks for at least some kind of judgement. I take it that you, Mr. Jeremy, you consider this not to be a way of leaving from your own free will and that you invite the witness to comment on that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy considers, under those circumstances, that people are not leaving from their own free will and wonders whether you have any comment on that position he takes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there was a dose of fear there. As for the rest, no comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, whether you do something of your free will or not is not a legal conclusion but indeed contains some judgement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, looking down this entry, we see at point 4 and then point 5 the following: "- Men in the sports hall, N. Front primary school." N. front is a reference to the Narodni front primary school; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the elementary school Narodni front.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see below that a reference to women and children in the sports ground. You see that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: When you say that you -- you could not say where the various persons who had been locked up in Sanski Most were at this time then, it's clear that, at least on the 28th of May, 1992, you were very clear where those persons were; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that they were detained at the front, at the sports hall, and the sports hall of the high school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when yesterday you said that you didn't know if civilians were captured and you didn't know where they were to be accommodated, then does this refresh your recollection that civilians were indeed captured and placed at these locations?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember when all these people were brought in and how many there were, women, children, men, et cetera. But I know that at that sports hall at that collection centre there was a medical team operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, yesterday it wasn't a question -- you didn't say you didn't remember when. You said you don't remember if they were at all captured and placed in these locations. Let's --

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time. I really cannot remember how all of that went.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's go to another entry in the -- in your diary, which is two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 29, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So this is an entry, sir, dated the 30th of May, 1992. It's again a Crisis Staff meeting. And I would like to focus your attention on the bottom half of the page where we -- we see below the reference to ten tractors, we read the words: "Civilians should be banned from entering destroyed neighbourhoods." And then two entries below that, we read: "- Collect all bodies in a single place." And below that: "- Exclude those who talk too much."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask you a question on those entries, sir. This reference to civilians being banned from entering destroyed neighbours and excluding those who talk too much, this -- this is an attempt to hide what had happened in places such as Mahala; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that civilians were banned from entering because of looting, because of looting the abandoned homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if the reason that they were not allowed to enter was because of looting, then why was it necessary to exclude those who talked too much?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were speculations. People were talking, saying all sorts of things, increasing, decreasing the number of casualties, victims, and that was supposed to be prevented. This kind of misinformation that was going out that was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, the final entry in this set of entries is the following: "- there is a possibility of addressing them in our uniforms." Now -- and I should note that the entry that precedes that at the top of the page refers to: "- They will come for the bodies at 09:00." Now, sir, this is an attempt to cover up the killing of unarmed civilians by making them look like military, is it not, by dressing them in military clothes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's the way it was. My proposal was that people who were at Hrustovo -- I mean, who were killed in fighting, whatever, they wore very little clothing. For two or three days, the corpses were out there in the open. Wild animals reached them. It had been raining. And I suggested that the people be dressed in a dignified manner, at least to be wearing dry and proper clothing. At the Red Cross, they said that there was no clothing and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, this diary entry is dated the 30th of May, 1992. Now that's -- that's at least a day before the men, women, and children in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje were killed. So this reference to "dressing them in our uniforms" has got nothing to do with Vrhpolje or Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the main thing was that the Red Cross had no clothes, and my suggestion was that we had clothing from the medical corps so that they would be buried in a dignified manner. That was not accepted, though. So they were buried as they were. And there was no intention to conceal anything nor is it possible to conceal anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So your position is that your suggestion to dress dead people in military uniforms was an act of charity?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object. Misstates the answer of the witness. The witness said "clothing from the medical corps," not military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the document says uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not military, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, military. That's a -- well, okay. Witness, could I ask you, where you refer to uniforms here, you said earlier that these were the uniforms that were available where, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what we had in the reserve. The medical corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were those military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was -- I mean, medical staff. Uniforms for medical staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's still military medical staff, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military medical, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is, military uniforms to be worn by those who are performing medical duties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I also get clarity here. You're saying the intention was to give these witnesses a dignified burial. Would you not regard as giving them a dignified burial also to make sure that they are buried in the presence of their relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be, but it was not possible. There were war operations, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have been humane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it was inhumane to do -- not to bury them in the presence of their relatives. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on to another entry in your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see a 31 at the top of the page, which might indicate the 31st of May. We see it's another Crisis Staff meeting. At number 5) Various, we see a reference to deportation towards Jajce should be carried out. We see a reference to military-aged persons should be sent to Manjaca. Now, sir, you're aware that many non-Serbs captured in Sanski Most during these operations were sent to Manjaca camp; yes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they were sent to Manjaca, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I should also clarify, this reference to deportation towards Jajce, that's a reference to the deportation of non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a reference to the evacuation of the civilian population to Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, the word is -- that I read is "deportation." Let's go to the next page, sir. Now, at the top of the page, we see a reference to: "The bridge under the Biscevic house has a basement ..." this is a reference to the house of the family of Faik Biscevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think this is a reference to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, there is evidence in this case that after he was taken into custody that the Biscevic home and businesses were looted and set on fire. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I heard that the house had been shelled. I know nothing about looting. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now you refer to the Biscevic family in your statement and you refer to his son who I believe was a dentist; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you say in your statement that he -- that his son, Haris Biscevic, and his father both had a role in the arming of Muslim units. And you say that before the war, Haris Biscevic told you that dentistry was going to belong to the Muslims and that it would bear the name of Biscevic. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He said that publicly in a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Faik Biscevic had three sons in total, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And all four of those Biscevic men were sent to Manjaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know where they were sent. I know that Faik was, but I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you a document in connection with this to see if it refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, coming up on our screens is a -- it's an article from the press, from the Sanski Most press, and it relates to the Biscevic family. It's dated the 20th of April, 2007. The article concerns the family and the death of one son at Manjaca, Edin, and the disappearance of another one of the sons, Haris, who you mention in your statement. Sir, we see that the picture of Nedin Biscevic together with his mother. Do -- you recognise those people; yes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedin Biscevic? No. And whether this is Jasminka, that's the other thing you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, if that's the name of Faik Biscevic's wife, then I'm asking if you recognise her.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mother, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do --

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Jasminka but I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing this particular article before?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, it -- very briefly, it explains that Nedin's twin brother, Edin, disappeared from Manjaca on the 7th of July, 1992 and that he was later identified through DNA in 2007. It also explains that his other brother Haris, who you mention in your statement, who was also taken to Manjaca, was still missing as of 2007. Now as regards Edin, who disappeared on the 7th of July, 1992, this Chamber has received evidence that on that date a number of men suffocated to death while being transported from Betonirka to Manjaca. Now, Faik Biscevic testified in the Brdjanin case that his son Edin disappeared after going to the aid of these men on the 7th of July, 1992. Did you know about Edin's disappearance?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You were, however, aware of these suffocations on the 7th of July, 1992, on transport that was going from Betonirka to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about that only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So the medical technician that you said was -- yesterday was at Betonirka, they didn't tell you about this particular event?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe this misstates the evidence. I believe the event did not take place at Betonirka, according to my recollection of the evidence, which has not been cited by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My question was whether the medical technician at Betonirka told the witness anything about that event which I don't think in any way misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you told us a medical technician was based at Betonirka. My question for you is whether that medical technician told you anything about these deaths in this transport that went from Betonirka to Manjaca on the 7th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a medical technician. Nobody informed me about any suffocations. I only learned about them later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were chief of the medical service in the 6th Brigade by the 7th of July, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So this was a convoy from Sanski Most to Manjaca military camp, a convoy on which many men died, they suffocated to death, and nobody got into contact with you in your capacity as the leading medical person in the 6th Brigade in the area from which these men originated; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the health centre was in charge of the transport of people to Manjaca. They were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were -- you yourself used to work at the health centre. You must have had very many contacts there. There are the series of meetings in your diary at the health centre. Nobody from the health centre told you anything about these events then; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to that time, I did not hear anything about that. It was only subsequently that I learned from the health centre -- or, rather, from some people at the health centre, that there were deaths due to suffocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps some ten days after the transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what steps did you take on hearing that in your capacity as chief of the medical service in the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. Because the military did not secure the transport. It was the medical health centre that was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So you didn't know about this event at the time. You heard about it only later. But you do know for certain that the military didn't secure the transport?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that the military medical service did not provide medical security for the transport. It was the health centre that was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31993 receives Exhibit number P7124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Jeremy, could I ask the witness -- You said: "I'm sure that the military medical service did not provide medical security for the transport." Who organised the transport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how do you know that the health centre was providing medical care for that transport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Grubisa told me that. He was the director of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any medical security during that transport? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know that because I did not participate in the exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Dr. Grubisa told you about providing medical care for the transport. What -- did he just in general terms say, "We provided medical care for the transport"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In general terms. He told me that the medical centre is in charge of escorting and providing the necessary medical assistance to the convoy en route to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not know anything about what medical security was provided for the transport at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't. But I believe that there were medical technicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the transport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there were teams of escorts and that some of them were medical technicians. I think that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How were these teams then composed? Who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you how the medical service was organised. As for the civilian branch, I really don't know how it was organised. The medical service in the army had battalions, brigades, and the medical service of the brigade. There was a company medical assistant, a battalion medical assistant, and a technician, and a brigade medical assistant and technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the organisation of the structure. Now, do you know, that transport, was there any responsibility for the military as far as you are aware of for that transport? Were they involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. But I believe there were few or none. If the military had been involved, they would have turned to me and requested medical escorts for the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless they would have failed to comply with their duties. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say if there were military involved, they would have come to me. Now, it may well be that they should have, but it doesn't mean that if there were any military involved that they, indeed, would have come to you. I'm just putting to you that that is a possibility as well and whether you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible but it doesn't make sense. I believe that they would have requested medical security if they had been in charge of the transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least if they were concerned about the health of those they were transporting. That is an assumption, I take it, which is at the basis of your observation. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly well and correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, we are moving to my final area now. Could we please go to page 42 of your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: 65 ter -- sorry, 19777. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, this entry is dated the 8th of June, 1992. It's another Crisis Staff meeting. And I want to focus -- I'd like to focus your attention on the conclusions of that meeting, and particularly number 4 which reads: "Move the Muslims and the Croats to the extent which would provide for a steady control of power." Now, sir, that reflected a decision reached at a meeting of representatives of the various municipalities in the ARK the day before; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that's P3753 in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you putting your questions to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My question is whether this reference to move the Muslims and Croats to the extent which would provide for a instead control of power reflected, to your knowledge, a decision reached the previous day at a meeting of representatives of the various municipalities in the ARK.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: ARK. Is that the Autonomous Province [as interpreted] of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. The Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not have any contacts with that body as a medical professional. I was not aware of any of their decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see at number 2: "The following persons are to be freed from the hall:" And the first category is: "- those who voted for Yugoslavia." So, sir, by reading that, my understanding is that if you did not vote to stay in Yugoslavia then you were to remain a prisoner in the sports hall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 46 in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, we see that this is dated the 10th of June, 1992. It's another Crisis Staff meeting. And point 1 refers to: "Transport of women and children." So this refers to the transport of these women and children out of Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we're moving quickly, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But could we go to page 48, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this is another Crisis Staff meeting on this same date, the 10th of June, 1992. And we read in the first bullet point: "- The job of deportation of a part of Muslim population failed. Lots of mistakes. "Proposal: "1. Appoint a person for the deportation of the part of population. "2. for the Crisis Staff president." Now, sir, there's evidence in this case - P733 - that on the 14th of June, so four days later, General Talic reported to the VRS Main Staff that the attempt to expel Muslim and Croat refugees in the region of the ARK, of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, to Central Bosnia had failed because of transportation difficulties and their resistance to leaving their places of residence. So, sir, my question is whether you were aware that the difficulties that we see that you were clearly facing in Sanski Most in expelling or deporting Muslims and Croats were also being communicated to the Main Staff as problems being experienced in the entire region of the ARK. Sir, should I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The question is whether you were aware that the difficulties that you faced in Sanski Most in deporting the Muslim population was also being communicated to the Main Staff as being a problem experienced across the entire region of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we read here - and I've already read it out - that there was this proposal to appoint a person for the deportation of part of the population. Now within a couple of weeks of this diary entry, a man called Bosko Banjac was appointed to form a commission for this very purpose; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bosko Banjac was appointed for the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3787 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, while this is coming up, I can tell you that they are the -- this document provides the conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most dated the 23rd of June, 1992. So we see the date there at the top left-hand corner, 23 June 1992, and we see that there are decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we look at the bottom of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see that: "All municipalities in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina are tasked to appoint one representative to deal with the matters of relocation and exchange of population and prisoners. The appointments should be faxed to Vojo Kupresanin." Kupresanin was the president of the ARK Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, following what I've just read out, we read: "In accordance with this, the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most municipality appoints Vlado Vrkes to the aforementioned duty."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we can also go to the second page in the B/C/S, please. If we could go to the bottom of the page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And then we see number 4: "Bosko Banjac is ordered to form a Commission for population migration consisting of 5 members." Now, sir, within a few months of this committee for population migration, it was -- this committee was facilitating the departure of thousands of non-Serbs out of Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to my final exhibit, 65 ter 31784, please. When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, 65 ter 31784. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, coming up on our screens are conclusions adopted at the 11th Session of the Executive Committee of Sanski Most Municipal Assembly and then now on our screens. So we see it refers to a session being held on the 14th of August, 1992. And we see "Conclusion." And below that, we see the report by Bosko Banjac, chairman of the relocation commission, on the course of the voluntary departure of the population from the area of Sanski Most was approved. We read that: "All persons who have expressed a wish to move out voluntarily and have the required documentation, i.e. a telex guaranteeing them accommodation, will be allowed to do so." Number 3, there is a reference to the first group of 3.000 people leaving. And number 4, we read they are to pay a thousand dinars. Now, sir, this document refers to people wanting to move out voluntarily. Now, the reality is, is that they were not moving out voluntarily. They were being expelled, as indicated in your own diary entry three months earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that they moved out voluntarily or under duress. I believe that there were both kinds of people and both cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, in the two hours that we've been talking, we've seen Muslim and Croat leaders were arrested, their neighbourhoods threatened, attacked, their homes destroyed, members of these groups killed or imprisoned, separated from their families, buried without their families, and your position is that their departure was voluntary; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe. Couldn't rule it out. Because everybody is afraid of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. It's time for a break. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- tendering the last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours. Thank you. And I also need to talk about the tendering of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that there is an issue of making a selection, a relevant selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I propose we wait until after the redirect because I will also be using some pages from the diary. I am not sure if they are all the same ones that were used by the Prosecution or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's understood. That's the usual procedure, that we wait what parts were used by the parties, and that then the final selection will be made and sought to be admitted by the party who tendered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the last document, which is still on the screen, this is a different matter, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, sorry I've conflated those two. I would like to tender 65 ter 31784, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31784 receives Exhibit number P7125, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. We take a break and will resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready, you may proceed with the re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to return to your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 65 ter number 19777, page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the first bullet point under disarming the population, says: "- not necessary to seize weapons if they own a valid permit." Did anyone at the Crisis Staff ever make a different proclamation in this regard or change this which is written here from this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of anything different. That anyone did anything different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, it was established during the cross that this meeting was in late May 1992. Can you tell us by that point in time had there been any incidents involving armed Muslim units in Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. There were incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea of about approximately how many incidents are we talking about? A few, a lot, one?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few, a few. The first soldier who was killed in Sanski Most was at the silo. It was a Polish man, a young man. I don't know his name. That was during the disarming. Then two policemen in the village of Trnovo were disarmed. That is the second incident that I know of. So it was sporadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could turn to page 18 in the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at bullet point 3. It says "Seize all weapons" by hook or by crook that doesn't seem to be consistent with the bullet point you are talking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. All illegal weapons. That's what's written here. All illegal ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have illegal in the B/C/S? Because the translation doesn't have. Can we be helped?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm told that the B/C/S has "illegal" [Interpretation] "All illegal weapons should be taken away."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Let's -- you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should ask for CLSS to redo that page of the diary once it's finally tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it -- yes, if it would be tendered. And I think it would be appropriate that the Prosecution ask for it, it being tendered by the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked if these persons who were being brought in, Adil Draganovic, Mirzet Karabeg, et cetera, if they were leading non-Serbs in Sanski Most and you said they were. Now, I want to ask you were all of the persons listed here leading members of the SDA political party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, by this time, late May 1992, was it already known in Sanski Most that the SDA was arming Muslims in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the question was very leading. But apart from that, it asked for a kind of a general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, it can't be leading if the statement already has information about he acknowledged that was done. And my last question is: Was that known at this time of this meeting. It's in the statement of the witness that they had knowledge that the SDA was arming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- people, and he says so in the book. So it's a follow-up of that to find out whether at this point in time that was already known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps -- but that's another aspect of the question. We would like to know what exactly then was known and, rather, facts than a general impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could further explore that, Mr. Ivetic. That certainly would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you've heard the Judges. Could you tell us at this point in time - that is, late May, the 25th of May, 1992 - what was known about the arming of the Bosnian Muslims in Sanski Most by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Green Berets were formed and the Patriotic League. There were units in town. There were 300 armed persons in Vrhpolje. That's like 50 per cent of the 6th Sana Brigade when it arrived in the territory of the Sanski Most. That is what is written in the book, "It is a Crime to Forget a Crime."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness -- Witness, that knowledge about arming of Bosnian Muslims, your source is the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not from the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, because your answer finishes by saying: "... that's what is written in the book."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 300 armed persons in Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there were units in town. Your answer consists of three or four elements. The first is Green Berets were formed and the Patriotic League. What do you know about that and what is your source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Green Berets established armed groups in the centre of town, and they turned them into units. And in the neighbourhoods where they were, they were in control. One was not allowed to walk around there at night, or, if so, it was risky. They did not appear in day-time, but during the night they would patrol different neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how did you learn about that? What was your personal observation? What did you learn from other sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I learned that from people. Nobody dared move about at night in the neighbourhoods where they were armed at night because the patrols that were in those neighbourhoods could be seen. They didn't really make an effort to hide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You learned that from persons "who I personally observed," that they were not allowed at night to move there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were people. Not 100 per cent but, say, 95 per cent Muslim population. And also there were Serb houses. They were saying what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take this second part of your answer -- one second, please. The second part was there were units in town. You have explained that. There were 300 armed persons in Vrhpolje. How did you learn that? Is that what you took from the book or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that there were armed people up there, but I didn't know the exact number. I found out what the figure was from the book, but I did know that there were armed people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That clarifies your knowledge. Now, what do you know? Because that was -- the question, what do you know about the arming itself? How did they get the arms, from whom did they get it, how did they get it, how many arms they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, everybody was getting armed. Who got weapons from where, that was hard to establish. But there were way too many weapons before the war started, and who got weapons in which way, that is something I don't know. At any rate, weapons did turn up in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Ivetic, you may continue. I'm just looking at your response to my observation, that you are putting a leading question. I leave it to that, because in the statement the witness didn't say that there was arming. He said that he heard something of the kind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your answers now you've talked about the centre of town and neighbourhoods where people could not go during the evening hours because of the presence of these armed Green Berets. Could you be more specific. Does that part of town have a name; and, if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly it was Mahala, Otoka, Muhici, that part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at P3294 with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 57 in the English and page 40 in the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the document, I can let you know that this is Mr. Rasula's diary again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could perhaps zoom in on the right-hand side of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That can make it easier for you to read it. And this is again the same meeting from the 25th of May, 1992 that we just looked at in your diary. And if we look at item number 4 down near at the bottom of the page in both versions, we see a reference to Adil Draganovic, that he is to be taken into custody. And next to that in parentheses, it says: "In Mahala, 30 pieces were returned that he failed to turn in." And now the pieces is referred to in B/C/S as "cijevi", I want to ask you what is your understanding of what is being referenced here, these 30 pieces or "cijevi" that were surrendered, that he - Mr. Draganovic - failed to turn in.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant are long-barreled weapons, rifles, PAPs, APs, I don't know what they meant. But anyway, it's long-barreled rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to the next page in both versions of Rasula's diary, it's at the top in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could focus on the left-hand side of the page. And in the English, it's just below the notation that says Djuro N. 82-444.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there is reference to a "Fedjad Karabeg owns a machine-gun, and his father a rifle. Goes to Pobrijezje to attend meetings." Now, do you know if there is any relation between Mr. Fedjad Karabeg mentioned here and Mr. Mirzat Karabeg, who was one of the persons on the previous page, to be brought into custody?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Fedjad Karabeg is. But there is just one Karabeg family in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now Pobrijezje. We've talked about that. The Prosecutor asked you a few questions about Pobrijezje, where it is in relation to Sanski Most. I want to ask you what was your understanding at this time of what types of meetings were taking place in Pobrijezje as referenced in this entry?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably they were meetings of the SDA, of their members. And most probably arming was discussed as well, in my assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your question asks for an opinion. Do you want to know what his understanding was or do you want to know what those meetings were about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: His understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you've answered the question, what you thought these meetings were about. Could you tell us on what your opinions, because they are opinions, apparently, are based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, if it's isolated, that meetings are held in Pobrijezje, outside town, and SDA members are present, it is logical that one can assume what it was that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if we can go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, before we go there, I'll ask a general question. You were asked by Mr. Jeremy yesterday if those who had weapons were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was at temporary transcript page 80, lines 11 through 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of any Muslim combatants who laid down their arms and what happened to them, for instance, in Golaja?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Golaja, people were taken prisoner, those who were, and then exchange of prisoners took place. There were also prisoners from the Serb army, and there was this bus of extremists from Vrhpolje, Golaja, that was sent to Bihac, and Serb fighters were freed. That was the exchange. Major Veljko Brajic was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could return to your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Number 19777, and if we can have page 23 of the same. And it is the fourth item -- fourth line from the top, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "- Military age men, exchange, one-for-one." First of all, what is this referring to -- who was the other party or other side to this exchange -- to these types of -- to this -- to the exchange that is referenced here?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said. Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says here: "- Military age men, exchange, one-for-one." With whom were they to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably for Serb fighters. One-to-one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ivetic. I wonder if it makes sense to get a date for this exchange in Golaja. It might just make the witness's evidence a little bit clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a suggestion, Mr. Ivetic, which you may follow up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you've heard the suggestion. Could you give us a time-frame for the exchange that you referenced in Golaja that Major Brajic undertook, I guess?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done immediately after the fighting in Vrhpolje, within a day or two. That exchange was certainly carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would just -- you earlier referred to a question put by Mr. Jeremy yesterday, that if those who had weapons were killed. I think the question was whether those who had weapons were to be killed, which is not -- the one describes a kind of an instruction; the other describes a factual situation. So if that's -- if you would agree with me, I don't think that it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you know how frequent or -- were there more of these exchanges of military-aged men or combatants, one-for-one, with the other side?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Sana municipality, that was the only exchange, as far as I know. As for other front lines, there were exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in regard to "asanacija" of the battle-field or sanitisation that you were asked about today, do you know what the prescribed procedure for burial of human remains of enemy combatants was pursuant to the relevant rules of "asanacija"?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Asanacija" involves the collection of dead bodies, counting them. There were joint burials after that. Then the removal of dead livestock, and then disinfection and deratization.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, what is the proper purpose behind "asanacija" or sanitisation of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, preventing the spread of diseases, infections.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what effect does timing have on the spread of diseases from deceased human corpses left in the open?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has to be done pretty quickly, because the more one puts it off, the more likely it becomes for infection to spread, as well as an epidemic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in response to some questions earlier today, you mentioned military medical uniforms. Can you please describe for us the colour or appearance of those medical military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military medical uniform meant that it was compulsory to wear a red cross in order for there to be a distinction from other soldiers, ordinary soldiers. So it had to be visibly marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what colour were those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended. Olive-green-grey to light blue ones, light blue ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you were asked about the convoy that went to Manjaca where some individuals suffocated and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would not mind, apparently you are moving to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are moving away from the uniforms. That red cross, where was that? Was that an epaulette or was that on the upper arm or -- could you tell us a bit more in detail where that red cross would appear on the uniform itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part - for the most part - it was on the arm above the elbow, although there were uniforms where it was in front so that it would be visible. And even on the back. But usually it was on the upper arm. And visibly so; it was quite big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you say "quite big," could you give us an indication of the size of such red cross insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's say 20 by 20 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication with your hands, approximately, how it is, so that we could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it attached to the uniform itself or was it a kind of a band around the arm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were both. There were those that were sewn on. And also when we needed more, they would be put on the sleeve as a separate band.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say the ones sewed on, they were 20 by 20 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked about the convoy of persons from Betonirka to Manjaca where some individuals suffocated, and you identified a doctor from the health centre that told you that the civilian health centre was in charge of the convoy. The question I want to ask you is: Would it be -- or have you ever heard of there being an instance where a convoy would have joint military and civilian medical escort?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, just a few more points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to 19777, again. And it was, I believe, page 46 in both versions. This doesn't appear to be the -- Could we try page 44. I apologise. It was the part where there was talk of the -- ah, it's -- are we in 19777? It is page 46 then. But I think that the -- the English is a different book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown this page by Mr. Jeremy in bullet point number 1. And I want to ask you what is -- if you could tell us what is the meaning of the reference here to "5-6 tonnes of explosives seized in," and then in the English it says "one word illegible." Could you give us some more information on that by looking at the Serbian original? What is being talked about here?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to look at the transcript in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not the transcript, sir. Your diary. The entry on the diary under number 1 where it says: "- 5-6 tonnes of explosives seized in ..." And then the next word is illegible for the translators, and I'm wondering if you can read your own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Demisevci. Demisevci. And then it says "explosive Vitez Gorazde." That means that the explosive is from Vitez, I suppose, or "vitezit."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall perhaps what this might refer to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who provided that information and whether it was 5 to 6 tonnes or not. This is the information that arrived, and I know nothing more about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm somewhat lost by the illegible word, what it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a place name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a place name, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a place name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is that the correct name that's written on the transcript, Damesevci.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Damesevci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Demisevci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that was the information given. Are you familiar with this geographical name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Demisevci is a village near Sanski Most. Demisevci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Well, at least it's very good to have a doctor who can read his own handwriting. That's very exceptional and I'm happy that -- thank you so much. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honour, if I can assist further, it's D-e, everything else is correct in the transcript except that it's "D-e" at the beginning, and that should hopefully correct everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, on this page in item number 2, there is information on "captured Black Shirts." What are we to understand this reference to mean, these black shirts?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know what black shirts means. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My last question then is in relation to page 48 and an item that was shown to you during cross-examination. At least I thought it was -- I'm sorry, page 49 in the ... And under item number 1, it says: "Appoint a person for the deportation of the part of population." What was your understanding of what "part of the population" is being referenced here?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the complete population but a certain number of people who were supposed to move out. That's the meaning of this phrase, "the part."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have any further understanding of how that part would be comprised? Who would comprise that part?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it was the extreme part or the extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Doctor, again I thank you on behalf of General Mladic and my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my redirect subject to, of course, discussing with plaintiff's counsel what we need to tender from the diary. I don't have an objection. We just need to figure out what pages would go in. And, of course, the one translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would agree on that, then -- we'll hear from you. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Jeremy to put some further questions to you, I would like to briefly revisit a matter which was addressed by both the Defence and the Prosecution and it is about the meeting that took place on the 25th of May and which you are referring to in your diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I read again the line you were questioned about. It reads: "In Mahala, 30 pieces were returned that he failed to turn in, and that apparently refers to Adil Draganovic." Now, you've explained to us what you understood the 30 pieces to be. It says "they were returned." Do you know who returned them to whom?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about weapons? If it says 30 pieces, a reference is made to 30 pieces of rifles. Draganovic had collected them, but he did not turn them in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then the line reads: "In Mahala, 30 pieces were returned that Draganovic failed to turn in." Now, Draganovic apparently did not turn them in. And now it says they were returned. But returned by whom to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand to whom. If weapons were collected, they should have been handed in at the premises of the Territorial Defence. If the population had unlicensed weapons and if those were collected, they were to be handed over to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I see that. And apparently Draganovic failed to do that. That's at least how I understand it. And now the line reads: "30 pieces were returned that he failed to turn in." Which suggests that the weapons then finally, well, were returned. But my question is: By whom were they returned to whom?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that Adil collected the weapons that people voluntarily surrendered. He collected 30 pieces but failed to hand them over where he was supposed to hand them over. And people did return weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's still not entirely clear to me. Last question. You explained what you understood to be the 30 pieces. On what basis did you say these were long-barreled rifles? Have you seen them? Have you -- what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see them. But everything evokes long-barreled rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a linguistic matter, Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then we'd like to -- apparently "pieces" gets a very special meaning, and if --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not "pieces" in B/C/S. It's "cijevi," which is barrels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which means barrels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means barrels?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. It's P3294, page 57, for Your Honours if you want to pull it up, and we can ask for that to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer, because you were rather specific in what type of weapons those were, you take that from the reference in your own notebook or do you have any additional knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just assume. I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For example, a hunting rifle has a long barrel as well. On the basis of what you read here, could you exclude this to include hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't claim that the 30 pieces did not include those as well. Probably not many, but an occasional hunting rifle is by no means excluded from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you can tell us that on the basis of the text you've written, that you'd take it that these were weapons with long barrels, such as rifles, but that you do not have any further specific knowledge about those weapons? Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic [sic], before you sat down, you referred to an exhibit P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's okay. We understand each other, Your Honours. Yes, Your Honour, I did see that the transcript did not have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- exhibit number. It's P3294 and the relevant page is page 57 in the English and page 40 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That being clarified. Mr. Jeremy, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P2889 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, I would like to just ask you a brief question in relation to your evidence in relation to the disarming process which you've discussed with Mr. Ivetic just now. Now on our screens is a -- it's a report on the process of the disarming paramilitary formations in Sanski Most public security area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can zoom in on the first two paragraphs, please. I realise it's not that clear. The document is dated the 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now focusing on just the second --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sorry, if we go to the second page in each document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We will see that it's -- this document is signed by SJB chief Mirko Vrucinic. Mr. Davidovic, you knew Mirko Vrucinic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my high school teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to the first page again, please, in each language. I'd like to focus on the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, directing your attention to the second paragraph, we read: "The action of peaceful disarming and surrendering of weapons was carried out in the period between 10 May and 25 May 1992. During that period, the Muslim and Croatian population handed over only hunting weapons and other legally owned weapons, but illegally obtained military weapons were not surrendered, and were concealed (buried) on the instructions from above." So, sir, I just want to clarify your position in respect to this particular paragraph in this document. Is it your position that it wasn't necessary for Muslim and Croats to hand in their legally owned weapons in Sanski Most but that they, nevertheless, did that voluntarily? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that that happened, but I'm sure that there were people who did it voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see the numbers of weapons that were handed in, which gives us an idea of the number of people who you believe voluntarily handed these weapons back. So just as one example, 195 hunting rifles. Sir, I think you've answered my question. I've got no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the Bench has no further questions for you either, Mr. Davidovic, this concludes your testimony. We would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague, for demonstrating that doctors can read their own handwriting, for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly turn into private session before we take a break. And we'll then expect the next witness to appear after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
