utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break and will resume at ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness be can be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just spoke with him and he never requested protective measures. Probably we filed something. I was informed by Mr. Ivetic that at one point of time we were not certain who would be protected and who would not be protected, so that's why only because -- to be cautious enough, we filed something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that the filing of the 3rd of November, Defence motion pursuant to Rule 92 ter, to admit the written testimony of Slavko Puhalic, which was filed confidentially, that the status can now be changed to public.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to respond to the inquiry the Chamber made in private session. I think I can do so without actually requiring us to go back into private session. And I would say simply that while the submissions were a little vague, nevertheless, under the circumstances, we do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And allows us to proceed. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to use the very brief remaining moment. The witness was advised of his rights under Rule 90(E) in the Karadzic case. In view of the questions I intend to put, I'd request that the same advice be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I leave it in the hands of the Defence whether they want this to be -- whether this advice would be given to the witness right from the beginning. I don't know what questions you further have on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not deem it necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll do it at the beginning of cross-examination. Witness, Mr. Puhalic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is handed out to you now. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, having consulted my colleagues, we think that it may be better to give the 90(E) warning right away so that it's valid for the whole of his testimony. I mean, it's valid anyhow. Witness, before you'll be examined by Mr. Lukic, I would like to draw your attention to one of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It is Rule 90(E), and I'll read it to you. "A witness," that's you, in this case. "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." This means that if you fear that a truthful answer might incriminate yourself, do not hesitate to address me and ask whether you can be relieved from the duty to answer that question. If that is clear to you, we'll proceed, and you'll first be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Puhalic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us your name for the record. Do it slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Slavko Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens 1D1631, please. And if the statement could be given in hard copy to Mr. Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I hesitate to intervene at this moment, but the last list we got --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a, sorry. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as often, has sensed my interest before I even got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We redacted one paragraph, so it's better to have 1D1631a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have that on our screen, I take it. And that's also the version of the statement that is now given to Mr. Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.text: Thank you. After the establishment of the Trnopolje collection centre, Slobodan Kuruzovic asked Mr. Puhalic to help him at the beginning of the establishment of that collection centre. At the beginning, he acted as a driver to Mr. Kuruzovic, but mostly he was in charge of procuring the food for the Trnopolje collection centre. Mr. Puhalic will explain that the primary purpose of the Trnopolje collection centre was to remove non-Serb civilians from the combat zone, keep them there for a while, first and foremost for their personal safety, especially at night. Non-Serbs were allowed to leave the Trnopolje collection centre, and they could freely go out after reporting to the guard and leaving a personal document. The capacity of the collection centre was limited. People slept at the school and in the cultural centre, in cars, tractor trailers, and so on. There was a kitchen that could cook a limited number of meals. That food was distributed to the most destitute. Some people cooked food individually. In the collection centre, medical assistance was provided in an infirmary where there were one or two physicians and also two or three nurses. There was also a Muslim doctor. There were no infectious diseases in the collection centre. The whole area where people were staying was open. Only the part where there was the school and the cultural centre, by the entrance to the complex, was surrounded by metal fence which was put up to 1 metre high. There were people of all ages and genders at Trnopolje. Nobody was brought to Trnopolje forcibly. Trnopolje was not fully surrounded by TO members. There were neither machine-gun nests nor firing positions with their barrels pointed at the collection centre. And that was the short summary statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Karadzic case in 2013. Did you tell the truth in that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you also gave a sworn statement in the Karadzic case. That statement was truthful, too?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to ask first about one point in that statement. On page 9 of your Karadzic statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Which has been uploaded as 65 ter 1D02291.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- you state: "I know that mosques and sacral monuments were destroyed in the territory of Prijedor municipality during the war, but I do not know who did that or whether someone ordered it." Now, first, it's correct that you do know that a number of mosques and Catholic churches in Prijedor municipality were destroyed during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn back to 1991. You mention in paragraph 2 of your statement that you were mobilised into the 343rd Brigade in November 1991. What were your duties in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I was a foot soldier. After that, I started driving an ambulance. Until the end I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "after that I started driving an ambulance," when did you start driving an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: In the month of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when you say "until the end," you mean until you returned from Croatia in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you were mobilised into the 343rd Brigade in November 1991 because --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, first, were you ever demobilised or released from service?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then that actually completes my questions about that topic, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know if it was until the very end of April or perhaps it was until mid-March, because I got ill so I was on sick leave for a while as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Two questions in regard of that. First, when you say "the very end of April or perhaps ... mid-March," that refers to the time that you were in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you say you were on sick-leave from a military obligation that you continued to have; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask briefly a few questions about the video that Mr. Lukic showed this morning. First, were you ever present when journalists visited Trnopolje yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you did not see that video being filmed or the events depicted in it in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it is this footage or was there another one depicting journalists. Perhaps these or some others. I can't recognise them. But I did talk to the journalists within the perimeter of the refugees camp. I did talk to the journalists. I spent some five or ten minutes in a conversation with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So a moment ago when you said you were not ever present when journalists visited Trnopolje, you intend to correct that answer and say that on one occasion, in fact, you were present when journalists visited Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Maybe I did not understand your question properly. You're asking me if I was alone, but I wasn't. There was always somebody else --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: -- another soldier or another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- let me try and ask very precisely because it seems we may have an interpretation issue: There was one and only one occasion when you were at Trnopolje camp - physically present, of course, with thousands of other people - and journalists visited the camp; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you are unsure whether that was the occasion depicted in the video we saw this morning; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about the camp now, and I'll move away from that topic for the moment. Now, Trnopolje camp was located in a village also called Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Trnopolje camp, yes. Or a refugee centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, the question was the camp was in a village. The name of the village was also Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There was no combat in that village in the summer of 1992, was there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Correct. I am not sure. I think that a lad was killed on the eve of the exodus, before the population fled. I think that one or two lads were killed in Trnopolje. Apart from that, there was no fighting at all. I believe that people of Orthodox faith, that they were actually of Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the people who fled Trnopolje, they were -- who fled the village, they were Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Are and who arrived in the camp, yes. There were others as well. Ukrainians or perhaps even Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 32030.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, as it comes up, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence, Exhibit P7029 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That in 1991 there were about, 2.667 Muslims in Trnopolje village. Now what will be coming onto the screen in a moment will be the 1993 Prijedor census results. And not all of the data has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 3 in the B/C/S. Perhaps I mean page 2. I do. Page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At line 30, we see Trnopolje. And looking in the middle of the page, under the column "Muslims," we see there are two of them in Trnopolje in 1993. It's correct that almost all the Muslims who had lived in Trnopolje village before the war were gone by 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I really can't say that. I can tell you what was going on in Trnopolje while I was there. What happened next, I don't know. I don't know how many people left and who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, you passed through the village on your way to and from Prijedor town; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were aware Muslims from the village were coming to Trnopolje camp; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you know that the people in Trnopolje camp didn't stay in Prijedor municipality or go back to their homes. They were sent out of the municipality either to Muslim territory or third countries; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly. But I know that many Muslims stayed in Trnopolje while I was still there. I don't know how many of them stayed, but they stayed in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32030 receives Exhibit number P7126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7126 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, I want to turn now to the time you yourself spent in Trnopolje camp. Now, you arrived there at the beginning of Trnopolje's operation; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you don't mention this in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting this late, I couldn't locate the document. If we can be informed. It's in the evidence now, but can we be informed who composed this document? Because we cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm happy to provide provenance information after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two questions. I think, first of all, who made the document, whether you can see that on the document itself; and, second, is provenance, is where did you get it from. Mr. Lukic, would it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I had this document in front of me in -- in timely matter, I would object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to admission of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you can revisit the matter and you can -- because I do understand, Mr. Traldi, you are done with the document itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You can revisit the matter and express any objections after the break, after you have learned from Mr. Traldi where it comes from and what it exactly is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, turning back to your time at Trnopolje, you don't mention this in your statement, but you claimed in your Karadzic testimony that you were at Trnopolje from around the time it began operating up until the 11th of June, 1992. You then went for a spa treatment, returned on the 17th of July, 1992, stayed for 10 or 15 days or perhaps until the 15th of August, and then you were sent back to your unit. Is that your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So when you make statements about conditions in Trnopolje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, "more or less" is a rather ambiguous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything Mr. Traldi said which is not accurate which you would now want to change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I can't remember whether it was on the 15th or the 16th or the 14th. It was a long time ago. I can't remember the exact date when I returned from treatment, but it was about that time. And then up to the month of August, either the 1st or the 2nd of August -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it's right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it's right, sir, that in your evidence you were gone from the 11th of June until a time in the middle of July; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. If my memory serves me well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the break time, and Mr. Mladic does not feel well again, if he can leave the courtroom as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I notice we're close to the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's time a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break anyhow. Well, first of all, Witness, we would take a break and we would like to see you in 20 minutes again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it now happened twice. And, of course, the Chamber always has some concerns. If there is anything you would like to either explain or tell us in private session, you are free to do that, of course, and we'll carefully listen to it. If you think there is no reason, we leave it entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we just express that if Mr. Mladic is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- unable to attend --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- answer Your Honours after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear from you after the break. We'll take a break and will resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that Mr. Mladic is or will be transported back to the Detention Unit. Is there anything you would like to add to that information, and if so would you like to do it in an open session or would you like to do it in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would prefer to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I put on the record that Mr. Mladic returns to the Detention Unit not feeling well. At the same time, Mr. Lukic, his counsel, his lead counsel, has declared in private session that he was instructed that -- to tell the Chamber that we should proceed in the absence of Mr. Mladic and that he explicitly gives his consent to proceed in his absence. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Traldi, was there anything you -- oh, I thought you might want to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If it's regarding the document we discussed at the end of the last session, I provided information to Mr. Lukic informally over the break and understood him to be reviewing it, which was why I hadn't been addressing it on the record, to give him time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since we'll most likely not finalise testimony of the witness today, Mr. Lukic, you also have three days to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalic, we'll continue. And to the extent you would be surprised that Mr. Mladic is not in the courtroom, it is with his consent that we proceed in his absence. Carefully listen to the next questions that will be put to you by Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off, we were trying to nail down your chronology at Trnopolje, and I want to focus on one date. In your Karadzic testimony, you were quite specific that it was the 11th of June when you left Trnopolje to go for the spa treatment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were gone for about a month?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 4 of your statement, you say: "I was not the deputy of Major Kuruzovic, the collection centre warden." Now, you say this because you know survivors of Trnopolje camp have identified you as being Major Kuruzovic's deputy; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Perhaps some of the people did assume that I was his deputy, but I was a foot soldier. I did not have any rank or anything. If anything, I was a logistics man because I was in charge of supplies -- or that's what I did the most, the supplies of food and water and things like that. I was like a link between Kuruzovic and the other men. I was the one who communicated with him the most. That's why I suppose that they assume that I was either his deputy or something of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You said: "I was in charge of supplies ... that's what I did the most." What other tasks did you have in the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you mentioned supplies a moment ago. In your statement, you said you would go to procure food "pursuant to the orders of my superior officer." When you say your superior officer, you meant Major Kuruzovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you refer in paragraph 21 of your statement to military guards at Trnopolje camp. Those guards were from the 43rd Brigade of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were from the 43rd or the TO. I didn't know where the people were from, but they came from the town. I can't make any assumptions as to who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, given your communication with Mr. Kuruzovic at the time, I'd like to look at one part of his OTP interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 31960, page 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, beginning in the middle of the page, he was asked: "What unit within the brigade provided these guards that were given to you to secure the facility?" He answered: "Well, from all the units of the Brigade, and then they would change; one day one unit, the other day the other, and so on." He was asked: "And who did you ask for this additional help, who did you go and speak and then obtain these guards?" He responded: "To the Commander of the Brigade." And he was asked: "Who was that?" And he responded: "Arsic." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you should explain to the witness why there is no B/C/S version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. This is Mr. Kuruzovic's interview with the Office of the Prosecutor with -- at -- I'm only aware of an English transcript and that's why I'm reading to you, and I'm sure Mr. Lukic will correct me if I've done it imperfectly. But what I've just read to you, first: The commander of the brigade, Arsic, that's Colonel Arsic, the commander of the 43rd Motorised Brigade of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then does this portion of your commander's interview refresh your recollection as to which military unit the guards at Trnopolje camp came from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, before we go into more detail about the camp, I want to talk about one specific person who was at Trnopolje who you discuss in your statement, Mevludin Sejmenovic. Now, you say you took Sejmenovic to Commander Kuruzovic and then Vojo Kupresanin came and took Sejmenovic to his sister's house. Now the Chamber has heard evidence from both Sejmenovic and Kupresanin. Both of them gave evidence that Kupresanin got Sejmenovic out of Omarska, not out of Trnopolje. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Sejmenovic was transferred from Trnopolje to Omarska via the military police stationed at Keraterm before this happened; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge as to how he got from Trnopolje to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe something -- maybe a translation issue, I don't know. Maybe the gentleman can take off his headphones and I will explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you understand the English language, Mr. Puhalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't understand it. I don't understand English. But I can explain this, this thing about Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first -- if you would take off your earphones for a second, please. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Traldi, as it was recorded, and as I heard, said "police station," and it was translated "military police station," so probably that could cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Military police was the word I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah. And Mr. Lukic is quite correct that that word doesn't seem to have made it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. So maybe that could cause some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But I suggest that Mr. Traldi, again, repeats his question, and then without any ambiguities, we'll hear the evidence of the witness on that question. Could the witness be assisted in putting on his earphones again. Yes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, what I'd asked you was, and I'll break it up. First: Sejmenovic was transferred from Trnopolje to Omarska; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge as to how he got from Trnopolje to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were you involved with transporting him from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm confused. The first question was: "Sejmenovic was transferred from Trnopolje to Omarska; right?" The answer was: "No." And then your next question was: "Do you have any personal knowledge as to how he got from Trnopolje to Omarska?" And then the witness said: "Yes." Now, on the one hand side, he says he was not. And then -- but then he can tell us how. What's confusing me at least. If you could seek clarification there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's what I was attempting to do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know where I'm confused and what is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I share that, Mr. President, and hopefully we'll all figure it out together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it to you to do it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Lucky me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, were you involved with transporting Mr. Sejmenovic out of Trnopolje yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't involved. But if I may explain, I can say how this happened. Mr. Kuruzovic got some list. How do I put it? A list, including members of the SDA and some military conscripts. And now -- well, there were people on this list that were being looked for, and I was supposed to look for that person in the camp, inter alia. Since I knew a few Muslim friends who were with me in Western Slavonia and then who returned there with me and they received threats, even that they'd been killed and they'd kill their families if they don't stay on in Kozarac, so they did not return to Western Slavonia, and that's how I tried to talk to them, whether they knew Mr. Sejmenovic, and they said yes. And they said that he was moving there. Sometimes he would be in the camp, sometimes he would not be there, sometimes he'd be in hiding. So after two or three days - I cannot tell you exactly - one of these men said that Sejmenovic was there in the camp, and I went to the man, perfectly normally, if I can put it that way, and I said, "Are you so-and-so?" He said, "Yes." And I said Mr. Kuruzovic wants to talk to you, and that was that. I drove him to Mr. Kuruzovic. And then for some two or three hours they talked. And then -- now, there were either two or three men. I think the army was looking for them or something. They were present there, too. And then Mr. Kuruzovic said to me that I should drive Mr. Sejmenovic to the police station in Prijedor, which is what I did. I put the four of them in the car and drove them over there. And nobody was mistreated. They had a normal, nice talk. They part nicely. And that's how Mr. Sejmenovic got to the public security station down there. And then probably from there, he was transferred to Omarska. I don't know how and I don't know what happened afterwards. But according to things that Mr. Vojo Kupresanin said, I found out that he was in Omarska and that he got him out of Omarska and took him to Banja Luka, and then I don't know. He ended up at his sister's or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you were asking your Muslim contacts about Mr. Sejmenovic, did they also tell you that there were prisoners in the camp helping him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, no, no. I didn't ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move to another topic then. Now, in your statement, you deny that the people in Trnopolje were detained there. And you say they came in cars, on tractors. Now, many of them were brought there on buses; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there. I cannot say whether I remember somebody arriving on a bus. But, for the most part, in the beginning, people came on foot, in cars, tractors, trucks - how do I put this? - there were quite a few vehicles there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's have 65 ter 17421.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a record kept by Autotransport Prijedor of transport carried out for the needs of the army, the Crisis Staff, and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 2 in both languages, 20th of July, 1992 at point 7 is what we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see nine trips, for instance, between Hambarine and Trnopolje for the needs of the army. That's -- Autotransport, that's a bus company; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what we see here, that reflects nine busloads of people being brought to Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which article? I mean, what is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The 20th of the seventh. It's the third date down. And I'm looking at the bottom point, the seventh one: Hambarine-Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so that says nine bus trips between Hambarine and Trnopolje by Autotransport; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, by the 20th you were back from the spa; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Roughly. I don't know exactly. Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: A few lines down, we see on the 23rd, second one, seven or more trips for the needs of the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's at the very bottom of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Seven or more trips for the needs of the police between Trnopolje and Carakovo. Again, you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where can we find the words for "the needs of the police."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The heading of the column, "milicija," is translated as "police."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so what Autotransport's records reflect is that they made seven more trips between Trnopolje and Carakovo -- seven or more, on the 23rd, again when you were back from the spa; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so I'd put to you, sir, that you couldn't have missed 16 busloads of people -- 16 or more busloads of people being brought to Trnopolje shortly after you returned from your spa treatment; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know, maybe. I can't remember a single bus. Not a single bus. I cannot remember being present, either in terms of getting people off the bus or probably -- well, maybe I wasn't there. Maybe I was out of Trnopolje. Maybe I was in Prijedor. I cannot remember. Maybe I was out getting supplied. Maybe I drove a Muslim --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: -- to Kozarac. Maybe I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- I think you've gone somewhat beyond the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17421 receives Exhibit number P7127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7127 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you drive to Kozarac often during that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not. If somebody -- I mean, some of these people who were there. I mean, if I was supposed to drive someone or if people left some food or had dug something in or left some food, sometimes I would drive somebody there and bring them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so you saw the houses that were destroyed in Kozarac, the mosques that had been destroyed or damaged by that point in the summer of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning back to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32031.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an aerial image taken after the war, and what we see here is the two roads - one snaking down from the left, one going up the middle - that bordered the camp on two sides; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you see the intersection of those two roads at the bottom of the image?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has received evidence that there was a check-point there in 1992. Do you recall what organisation manned that check-point?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But you recall the check-point; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the check-point was somewhere -- from the direction of Kozarac, I think it's before the school, that there was this check-point there. I mean, people would be stopped so that they could not get through - I mean, not to say Serb people - so that they could not get close to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And there would be --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: There was a barrier there of sorts. Was it a log or something like that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And there would be guards at the check-point; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if you were going to stop people from getting through, you would need weapons, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, probably, guards had weapons but -- well, I'm not going to say -- well, that they were -- well, maybe they had these weapons next to them. It wasn't that they were holding them. I don't know. But they probably did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: They must have held them sometimes; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: A war is a war. And as people say, weapons probably had to be carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if you could just mark on the image with KP for check-point where you recall it being.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mentioned a school. That's the building immediately across the street; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you circle that and mark it with an S.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And one of these buildings is the Dom at Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you circle that and mark it with a D.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you had a room downstairs in the Dom that you used when you would speak with people detained there; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we see a lot of open space around these buildings. People held in Trnopolje would sleep in the buildings and lots of them would also sleep in makeshift tents or outside in that open area; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in the school, in the Dom, and in tents, trucks, cars, tractors, people tried in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I mean, I think, even over there in this area where the store was, people would sleep there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they slept outside because, of course, these buildings aren't large enough to house the thousands and thousands of people who passed through Trnopolje camp in the summer of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they dug latrines outside because the school and the Dom didn't have sufficient toilets for thousands of people; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you mention a clinic in your statement. Could you circle that and mark it with a K.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, right now, I cannot actually find my way here. I think it's this little building here within the Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, personnel there included Dr. Idriz Merdzanic and a veterinarian named Azra Blazevic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think the name is Azra Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Dr. Merdzanic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Probably. I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Vasif Gutic, a Serb medical student, also helped in the clinic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that was a medical student, but there was one medical technician or two. I cannot remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you mention this in your statement. You know, of course, because you had a room you used in the next building over that this was, in fact, a makeshift clinic that didn't have adequate supplies for thousands of detainees; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. What was there in the medical field, I really didn't know, wasn't my concern. I think it was Dr. Ivic, who was an ethnic Serb doctor from Prijedor who was in charge. But I did go there if somebody needed something, if they needed some kind of help. So, of course, we would see each other but I don't know exactly what they had. As regards this medical part, I cannot go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Probably they did not have enough --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now Dr. Ivic was with the Serb Red Cross and based across the street; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly where he was based. I cannot remember. But opposite -- well, I don't know whether the Red Cross was there. Dr. Ivic, was he at Major Kuruzovic's? I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: But he was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now there wasn't very much food in Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you're aware that detainees were killed in Trnopolje camp; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, was it one or two cases? That's something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, it was a lot more than one or two cases, wasn't it? The Chamber has received evidence that six members just of the Foric family were killed there -- or taken from the camp and killed, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot make any claims because I don't remember that. I'm just speaking about what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as far as you know, there were never any investigations into the killings that were committed at Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I think -- well, I don't know. On one occasion I know that Kuruzovic left, and I think there were two men. A soldier took them to get something -- was it food or something? Now, how far away did they go from the house? Somebody came up and then somebody was shot and then the soldier came back and said what happened. And the next day, I took Major Kuruzovic to the police station to have this investigated. And -- well, I'm not sure now. Two men, was it? I think Kuruzovic gave --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: -- them IDs, passes, so that they could go with the man --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll tender this image as marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32031, as marked by the witness, receives Exhibit P7128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter 32005, page 34. This is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can deal with that in two or three minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can. Okay. Then we'll proceed before we adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's his Karadzic testimony. There are portions under seal. This isn't one of them. Perhaps I was overoptimistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you were asked, beginning at line 18, and again this transcript is only in English so I'll read to you. You were asked: "Neither were any investigations conducted in relation to the killings that occurred in the camp or the beatings that occurred in the camp; that's right, isn't it? To your knowledge there were never any investigations?" And you said: "Well, as far as I know, no." That's the truth, what you said in your Karadzic testimony, that you don't know of any investigations into the murders committed at Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you that I know that Mr. Kuruzovic went up there. And now whether something was started after that, I don't know. But I do know that he went there to see what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I appreciate that clarification. Now, you also knew rapes were committed in Trnopolje camp, and you don't know of anyone that was ever prosecuted for any of the rapes that were committed in Trnopolje; do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke about that in Mr. Karadzic's case, too, that I only found out about one of these rapes. I didn't hear anything about the others. And when I heard about that, Dr. Ivic and Major Kuruzovic were informed, and orders were issued to go there. I went to the military police and to the SUP. Two military policemen went there, three policemen, and I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to stop you. You're repeating material that's in your statement. I asked you a very specific question. You don't know if anyone was ever prosecuted for committing rape at Trnopolje; do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Traldi, we should be clear. In our language, "prosecution" means to bring someone before a court. You are not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you still --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If I might still have just one minute, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at our interpreters, whether minute is, Mr. Traldi -- okay. You have an okay, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you still live in Prijedor, sir, so you know that today in front of where of Trnopolje camp was, there is a memorial to fallen VRS soldiers and no memorial to the people you know were killed and raped in Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PUHALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is a good point to break for the weekend, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before you leave the courtroom, I want to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever it may be about your testimony, testimony you've given already today or testimony still to be given, and we would like to see you back Monday morning at 9.30. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, as far as your last question is concerned, what is the relevance and probative value of what you apparently were seeking on whether there are memorials for one group and not for another?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think, in part, the witness resiling from the proposition, reflects on his credibility, among other things. So I'd begin with that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not because you consider him to in any way to be responsible for what kind of memorials were erected, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I certainly hadn't suggested that he was responsible for erecting memorials in Prijedor, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We adjourn for the day and will resume Monday, the 16th of February, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
